newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso must act fast to quash new crisis -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso must act fast to quash new crisis -analysts.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso risks serious delays to his reform programme unless he acts fast to quash allegations that a close aide was linked to a money-for-votes scheme, analysts said on Wednesday.

They said the evidence tying influential Communications Minister Sergio Motta to vote buying in Congress was weak, but the fallout to a brewing scandal would be disastrous if it was confirmed that he played a central role in the affair.
"All we've heard so far is gossip, nothing hard. But politics doesn't need hard facts, it functions in an environment of hyper-reality," said Brasilia-based political consultant Murillo Aragao.

The nation's capital has been reeling since Tuesday when the daily Folha de Sao Paulo published a transcript of a telephone conversation in which a congressman said he had received $188,000 to vote in favour of a constitutional amendment that would allow Cardoso to run for reelection.

On Wednesday Folha published new transcripts in which another congressman said he also had received money to vote for the reelection amendment, and that the funds had been paid with Sergio Motta's blessing.

A close personal friend and private business partner of Cardoso's, Motta is considered among the most influential members on the president's cabinet. Besides overseeing the $80 billion privatisation of Brazil's telecommunications system, Motta is the president's chief political operator and the architect of his reelection bid.
Analysts said that, if confirmed, the allegations of corruption at the highest level of government would be a first for the Cardoso administration.

While the government's economic reform drive has met stiff resistance from those opposed to his plans to open up the economy and slash spending, Cardoso has enjoyed high personal approval ratings largely as a result of his spotless reputation for integrity.

The latest scandal could change all that. "There is a novelty in Brazilian politics: for the first time since he took office in 1995, the honour of Fernando Henrique Cardoso's government has been put in doubt," Folha de Sao Paulo editor Josias de Souza wrote in a newspaper column on Wednesday.
Analysts said the new scandal was particularly worrying because it could mean the president would be forced to backtrack in his plans to seek a second term in office.
"What people want to know is how close will this hit the top people in government," said Craig Barley, commercial manager at Banco Omega.
Opposition congressmen have moved fast to collect the required 171 signatures to put together a Parlimentary Investigative Committee (CPI) which could be ready before the end of the day.

Government allies privately admit a CPI is probably inevitable. However they said their plan would be to pack the committee with their own people to ensure the probe is swift and brief. They said the government is determined the new crisis will not derail the reform programme.
Analysts said it was still too soon to measure the full impact of the scandal, although they hoped to get an idea when Congress prepares for a series of important votes scheduled for Tuesday evening.
"Let's see how Congress behaves. The voting this eveining will serve as an important indicator for the crisis," said Carlos Lopez of Brasilia's Santa Fe Ideas consulting group.
